subject: language_arts

unit.title: Spelling with suffixes
unit.essentialQuestion: How do I add an ending to a word so it's still spelled correctly?

title: y → i (happy → happier)
objectives: By the end, I can change a final y to i before -er/-est/-ed (but keep y before -ing).

vocabulary.definition: the main word before any ending
vocabulary.example: happy is the root of happier

vocabulary.definition: a little ending (tail) added to a word
change the final y to an i before adding the suffix
a special case that breaks the rule

emphasize: When a root ends in y, change the y to i before -er, -est, -ed.
The one exception that MUST be flagged: keep the y before -ing (we never want ii — crying, not criing).
Pre-empt 'happyer'/'cryed' (kept the y). Repeated image: the y TRANSFORMS into an i.

keyConcepts: y-ending roots change y to i before -er/-est/-ed
the -ing exception: keep the y (no double i)
checking the suffix FIRST decides whether the y transforms
misconceptions: keeping the y: happy + er → 'happyer', cry + ed → 'cryed'
over-applying the rule before -ing: cry + ing → 'criing'
applying the y rule to a word with no y (sad is a doubler → sadder)
hooks: The y TRANSFORMS into an i like magic — but before -ing it refuses to change, because two i's in a row look wrong.
priorKnowledge: the earlier suffix rules: just-add (L5), drop-e (L6), double (L7)

digital: animated whiteboard showing the y transforming into i
side-by-side contrast of cried vs crying

plan.goal: Feel 'happyer' fail, watch the y transform into an i, and preview the -ing twist; retrieve Lesson 6.
plan.note: Two tricks in one lesson — flag both in the hook so the twist doesn't blindside later.
plan.successCriteria: Child answers 'drop the e → hoping' for the retrieval and is curious about the transformation.

script.say: Happy plus -er — is it happyer? Read it… nope, that's not right. Watch the magic: the y TRANSFORMS into an i — happi-er — happier! But watch this twist: with -ing, the y stays put — crying, not criing. Two tricks in one lesson. Ready? First, quick memory check — we've learned three suffix tricks already. What do we do to hope before -ing?
script.adaptHints: Listen for: drop the e → hoping. If shaky, quick recap: just-add (jump), drop-e (hope), double (hop) — 'today is a fourth trick, for words ending in y.' Mime the transformation with your hands.

stuckProtocol: If the retrieval is shaky: one-line recap of each earlier trick with its example word (jump, hope, hop), then straight back to happy.

plan.goal: Teach the rule + exception: y → i before -er/-est/-ed; keep y before -ing. Model happy → happier/happiest, cry → cried BUT crying.
plan.note: Build cried and crying side by side — the contrast carries the exception.
plan.successCriteria: Child can say both parts back: change y to i, except keep the y before -ing.

script.say: Rule: if the root ends in y, change the y to i before -er, -est, -ed. Watch happy: change y to i, add -er → happier; add -est → happiest. Now cry: change y to i, add -ed → cried. BUT — big exception — keep the y before -ing, because two i's look wrong: cry + -ing = crying, NOT criing. So: y to i for -er, -est, -ed; keep y for -ing.
script.adaptHints: Repeat the two-part rule rhythmically: 'y to i… except before -ing.' Let the child cross the y and write the i themselves in the air.

elements.value: y → i for -er / -est / -ed … keep y for -ing

plan.goal: Shared transforming: funny + er, sunny + est, try + ed — then the twist: try + ing keeps the y.
plan.note: The child announces what happens to the y BEFORE spelling. End on the -ing twist so it's fresh.
plan.successCriteria: Child says 'change it to i' unprompted for -er/-est/-ed, and 'keep it' for -ing.

script.say: You make the change. Funny plus -er. What happens to the y? … That's it — funnier! Now sunny plus -est… and try plus -ed. And here comes the twist: try plus -ing. Careful — what does the y do this time?
script.adaptHints: If the child changes the y before -ing, don't correct directly — write 'triing' and ask them to read it. Two i's look wrong; the y stays.

wrongAnswers.why: kept the y
wrongAnswers.remedy: Read it — happy-est? The rule says change the y to i before -est. Cross the y, write i.

wrongAnswers.why: changed y to i but doubled the i
wrongAnswers.remedy: Just ONE i — the y becomes i, then -est joins on: happi + est.

plan.goal: The key diagnostic: happy + est. 'happyest' means the y survived; also guard the -ing over-application.
plan.note: After a correct answer, probe: 'What did the y do?' (turned into an i).
plan.successCriteria: Child spells 'happiest' and states the transformation.

script.say: Add -est to happy. Remember the magic.
script.adaptHints: After success, probe: 'What did the y do?' Then a lightning bonus: 'and before -ing, what would the y do?' (stay).

blocks.explain: The y transforms into an i, then -est joins on: happiest.

wrongAnswers.why: kept the y
wrongAnswers.remedy: Read it — happy-est? The rule says change the y to i before -est. Cross the y, write i.

wrongAnswers.why: added the i without removing the y
wrongAnswers.remedy: The y doesn't get a partner — it TRANSFORMS. Cross the y out, the i takes its place.

wrongAnswers.why: lost a letter in the swap
wrongAnswers.remedy: Careful — only the y changes. happ-i-est: the double p stays, the i replaces the y.

plan.goal: Independent spelling: happiest, sadder (decoy — a doubler!), dried, flying (the -ing exception), each read back.
plan.note: Director draws from practiceBank, start level 2. The sad decoy and the flying exception are the highest-value items — make sure both appear.
plan.successCriteria: Child changes y → i in at least three words, keeps the y in flying/crying, and spots that sad has no y.

script.say: Your turn, transformer! I'll send you words. Check the suffix FIRST — is it -ing? Then the y stays. Anything else — the y turns into an i. And watch out: one of my words is a sneaky imposter with no y at all!
script.adaptHints: Frame feelings words around the child's world (their happiest day, the funniest joke) — the spelling words never change.

stuckProtocol: Name why: 'the y needs to change' or 'before -ing the y stays.'
Step down: give the pair side by side (happy → happi__) so the child copies the change.
ONE hint: 'is the suffix -ing? If not, change y to i.'
Re-ask a smaller version (just one word), then build back up.
Keep it safe: 'The -ing twist is tricky for everyone — let's check the suffix first.'

plan.goal: Child teaches back the rule AND the twist; end on an earned win.
plan.note: Child-led. All four rules now learned — tease Lesson 9's Sorting Office.
plan.successCriteria: Child states: change y to i before -er/-est/-ed; keep the y before -ing.

script.say: Teach me the y rule — and don't forget the twist. … Perfect. You transformed the y into an i every time — and you remembered the tricky -ing twist that catches lots of people out. That's all four suffix tricks learned — next time you become a Sorting Office worker and use them ALL!
script.adaptHints: Process praise the suffix-checking habit. Preview, don't teach, the Lesson 9 sort.

blocks.prompt: Say the whole rule out loud: 'y to i — except keep the y before -ing!'
blocks.target: y to i, except keep the y before -ing

wrongAnswers.why: kept the y
wrongAnswers.remedy: Read it back — funny-er? The y needs its magic. What does it turn into before -er?

wrongAnswers.why: added the i without removing the y
wrongAnswers.remedy: The y transforms — it doesn't stay for the party. Cross the y, the i takes its seat.

hints: The suffix is -er — not -ing — so the y transforms.
Cross the y, write i, then add -er.

reteach.say: Funny wants to grow: cross the y — funn — the i steps in — funni — add -er: funnier! Your jokes just got funnier.

block.explain: The y transforms into an i: happi + est = happiest.

wrongAnswers.why: kept the y
wrongAnswers.remedy: Is the suffix -ing? No — so the y must change. What does it become?

wrongAnswers.why: kept the y AND added an i
wrongAnswers.remedy: It's a swap, not a squeeze — the i REPLACES the y. happi + est.

hints: -est is not -ing — so the y changes.
happi… then -est.

reteach.say: The happiest day! Happy: the y transforms — happi — then -est: happiest. Say the two beats of the change: happ-i… est.

block.statement: Before -er, the y in happy changes to an i.
block.explain: Yes — y → i before -er, -est and -ed. Only -ing lets the y stay.

wrongAnswers.why: hasn't fixed the y → i rule yet
wrongAnswers.remedy: Try writing happyer and reading it back — does it look right? What fixes it?

hints: Remember happier from the hook.
The y transforms before -er, -est, -ed.

reteach.say: The y rule in one breath: y turns into i before -er, -est and -ed — happy → happier. The only tail that lets the y stay is -ing.

wrongAnswers.why: kept the y
wrongAnswers.remedy: Check the suffix — is it -ing? No! So what happens to the y?

wrongAnswers.why: changed the y but lost one n
wrongAnswers.remedy: Only the y changes — the twin n's in sunny both stay. sunn-i-est.

hints: The suffix is -est — the y transforms.
Keep both n's: sunni + est.

reteach.say: The sunniest day of the year! Sunny: cross the y — sunn — i steps in — sunni — add -est: sunniest. Everything else in the root stays put.

wrongAnswers.why: kept the y
wrongAnswers.remedy: Read it — try-ed? Before -ed the y transforms. Cross it, write i: tri + ed.

wrongAnswers.why: kept the y and lost the suffix's e
wrongAnswers.remedy: Two fixes needed: the y becomes i, and -ed keeps its e. tri + ed = tried.

hints: -ed is not -ing — so the y changes.
tri… then -ed.

reteach.say: Yesterday I tried my best! Try: y transforms — tri — add -ed: tried. Short and neat — t-r-i-e-d.

wrongAnswers.why: over-applied y → i before -ing
wrongAnswers.remedy: Read it — fl-i-i-ng? Two i's in a row look wrong. Before -ing, the y STAYS.

wrongAnswers.why: invented an e to glue the parts
wrongAnswers.remedy: No glue needed! Fly keeps its y, -ing joins straight on: flying.

hints: Check the suffix FIRST — it's -ing!
Before -ing the y stays put.

reteach.say: The twist! Before -ing the y refuses to change, because criing and fliing with two i's look wrong. Fly + ing = flying, y proudly staying. Same for cry → crying, try → trying.

practiceBank.skill: match roots to suffixed forms across the rule + exception

block.prompt: Match each build to its correct spelling.

wrongAnswers.why: matched the -ed form to the -ing build
wrongAnswers.remedy: Check the tail on the build — -ing keeps the y. Which answer still has its y?

wrongAnswers.why: kept the y before -ed
wrongAnswers.remedy: -ed is a transformer tail: the y becomes i. Which spelling shows that?

hints: Find the -ing build first — its answer keeps the y.
All the others transform y → i.

reteach.say: Sort by the tail! One build has -ing — trying, y stays. The other three have -er, -est or -ed — so their y's all turned into i's: happiest, dried, funnier.

practiceBank.skill: spot when the y rule does NOT apply

block.text: sad + er = ___ (careful — is there a y?)

wrongAnswers.why: applied the y rule to a word with no y
wrongAnswers.remedy: Look at the end of sad — is there a y to change? What kind of word is s-a-d (one short vowel, one consonant)?

wrongAnswers.why: forgot Lesson 7's doubling rule
wrongAnswers.remedy: Read it — say-der? The short a needs protecting. What does the d do before -er?

hints: Check the end of sad — no y here!
One short vowel + one consonant… which rule is that?

reteach.say: Imposter alert! Sad has no y — it's a short-vowel word, so it uses Lesson 7's trick: double the d. Sad → sadder. Always look at the END of the root before choosing the rule.

block.explain: Before -ing the y stays — crying. Two i's in a row look wrong.

wrongAnswers.why: over-applied y → i to the -ing exception
wrongAnswers.remedy: Look at criing — two i's in a row! That's exactly what the exception avoids. What does the y do before -ing?

hints: Count the i's in criing — what do you notice?
Before -ing the y stays.

reteach.say: The whole reason for the twist: English hates ii. If cry's y changed before -ing we'd get criing — yuck! So the y stands its ground: crying. y → i everywhere EXCEPT -ing.

block.prompt: Why does crying keep its y, but cried changes to an i? Explain like a spelling teacher.
block.sample: Before -ing we keep the y so we don't get two i's in a row (criing looks wrong). Before -ed the y changes to i: cried.

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: Keeping the y before -ing avoids a double i (criing); before -ed the y changes to i (cried)

wrongAnswers.answer: They're just random / you have to remember
wrongAnswers.why: hasn't connected the exception to the double-i reason
wrongAnswers.remedy: Write criing and look at it. What do you see in the middle? That's the reason the y stays.

wrongAnswers.why: shares the kept-the-y misconception
wrongAnswers.remedy: Which suffix is on cried — is it -ing? No, it's -ed — so the y transforms. Only -ing lets it stay.

hints: Try writing criing — what looks odd?
The exception protects us from double letters that confuse readers.

reteach.say: Here's the teacher's secret: the -ing exception isn't random — it exists so we never write ii. Cried gets the transform because -ed causes no clash. Crying keeps the y because -ing starts with i, and ii looks broken. One reason, whole rule explained.

adaptivity.levelUp: 2 consecutive correct at the current level → next level; at level 3, interleave the sad decoy and the -ing exception with straight y → i items.
adaptivity.levelDown: 2 misses on the same skill → run the item's reteach with the pair written side by side (happy → happi__), then a level-1 item.
adaptivity.masterySignal: 3+ correct across levels 2–3 including one -ing exception (flying/crying kept the y) and the sad decoy → mastery ≥ 0.8 for 'y → i before a suffix'.
struggleProtocol: Name why: 'the y needs to change' or 'before -ing the y stays.'
Step down: give the pair side by side so the child copies the change.
ONE hint: 'is the suffix -ing? If not, change y to i.'
Re-ask a smaller version (just one word), then build back up.
Keep it safe: 'The -ing twist is tricky for everyone — let's check the suffix first.'
adaptivity.personalization: Use the child's happiest/funniest/sunniest real moments in the sentences around the words — the spelling words never change.
adaptivity.endOnSuccess: Finish on a winnable y → i item; process praise: 'you checked the suffix first every time — that's exactly how spellers beat the twist.'

differentiation.support: Pairs given side by side (happy → happi__) so the child copies the change and adds the suffix. Avoid the -ing exception until the main rule is secure.
differentiation.stretch: Explain WHY crying keeps the y (we don't want ii) and spell trying, drier, busiest.

extension: Find two more y-ending words (lucky, dirty) and make them into 'more/most' words (luckier, dirtiest).
assessmentEvidence: Child correctly changes y → i in at least three words (happiest, cried, sadder) and keeps the y in flying/crying.
revisitLater: Include happier/happiest and crying in the Lesson 9 sort; bring back the -ing exception as a quick check next session.
